claim: The right V1 of monkey K was surgically removed by aspiration 46 months before the present experiments.
source: The right V1 of monkey K and U, and left V1 of monkey T was surgically removed by aspiration, 46, 44 and 6 months before the present experiments, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text describing the timing of V1 lesion surgery for monkey K.

claim: The right V1 of monkey U was surgically removed by aspiration 44 months before the present experiments.
source: The right V1 of monkey K and U, and left V1 of monkey T was surgically removed by aspiration, 46, 44 and 6 months before the present experiments, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text describing the timing of V1 lesion surgery for monkey U.

claim: The left V1 of monkey T was surgically removed by aspiration 6 months before the present experiments.
source: The right V1 of monkey K and U, and left V1 of monkey T was surgically removed by aspiration, 46, 44 and 6 months before the present experiments, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement in the manuscript text describing the timing of V1 lesion surgery for monkey T.

claim: The lesion area was confirmed by MR images.
source: The lesion area was confirmed by MR images and the range of the lesion-affected visual field was confirmed by increased threshold for detecting saccadic targets at the beginning of the present experiments (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to MR images shown in figures.

claim: The range of the lesion-affected visual field was confirmed by increased threshold for detecting saccadic targets at the beginning of the present experiments.
source: The lesion area was confirmed by MR images and the range of the lesion-affected visual field was confirmed by increased threshold for detecting saccadic targets at the beginning of the present experiments (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement describing behavioral testing to confirm visual field deficits.

claim: Luminance contrast sensitivity of all targets to induce saccadic eye movements clearly decreased in affected visual field.
source: We presented targets at possible positions which covered the whole contralesional visual field (monkey K; 3 directions × 3 eccentricities, monkey U; 5 directions × 4 eccentricities, monkey U; 5 directions × 3 eccentricities) and luminance contrast sensitivity of all targets to induce saccadic eye movements clearly decreased in affected visual field (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The visual deficits caused by these lesions was similar to the animals which were reported previously by Yoshida et al., 2008.
source: The visual deficits caused by these lesions was similar to the animals which were reported previously (Yoshida et al., 2008).
evidence: Direct comparison to previously published work.

claim: The V1 lesion affected most of the contralesional visual field, at least from 5° to 15° eccentricities.
source: These results indicated that the V1 lesion affected most of the contralesional visual field, at least from 5° to 15° eccentricities.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing the extent of visual field deficits based on behavioral testing.

claim: Visual input pathways from retina can be classified into two major pathways; one is cortical pathways via LGN and V1, the other is subcortical pathways via the SC.
source: Visual input pathways from retina can be classified into two major pathways; one is cortical pathways via LGN and V1, the other is subcortical pathways via the SC.
evidence: Statement of established anatomical knowledge about visual pathways.

claim: The monkeys with unilateral V1 lesion were used to investigate abilities of the subcortical visual pathways through the SC.
source: The monkeys with unilateral V1 lesion were used to investigate abilities of the subcortical visual pathways through the SC (Mohler and Wurtz, 1977; Kato et al., 2011; Takaura et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental rationale with supporting citations.

claim: The V1 lesion allowed assessment of contribution of visual information via the SC to support visual classical conditioning and to evoke phasic DA responses following the presentation of conditioned stimuli.
source: In this study, the V1 lesion allowed us to assess contribution of visual information via the SC to support visual classical conditioning and to evoke phasic DA responses following the presentation of conditioned stimuli.
evidence: Direct statement of the experimental purpose and design.

claim: After 12 days of having the CSs predict juice delivery (approximately 200 trials/day), conditioned anticipatory licking was induced by both LR-CS and SR-CS.
source: After 12 days of having the CSs predict juice delivery (approximately 200 trials/day), conditioned anticipatory licking was induced by both LR-CS and SR-CS (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral results with reference to supporting figures.

claim: The conditioned licking rate during the CS presentation was significantly higher in LR trials than in SR trials in 15 sessions in monkey K.
source: The conditioned licking rate during the CS presentation was significantly higher in LR trials than in SR trials (15 sessions in monkey K and 16 sessions in monkey U, Figure 1D, α <0.05, Wilcoxon signed-ranks test).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with specific test and significance level.

claim: The conditioned licking rate during the CS presentation was significantly higher in LR trials than in SR trials in 16 sessions in monkey U.
source: The conditioned licking rate during the CS presentation was significantly higher in LR trials than in SR trials (15 sessions in monkey K and 16 sessions in monkey U, Figure 1D, α <0.05, Wilcoxon signed-ranks test).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with specific test and significance level.

claim: The conditioned responses elicited by CSs presented to either the intact or lesion-affected visual fields were not reliably different.
source: In addition, the conditioned responses elicited by CSs presented to either the intact or lesion-affected visual fields were not reliably different (Figure 1E), (α <0.05, two sample t-test with Welch's correction).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with specific test and significance level.

claim: A visual cue presented in the V1 lesion-affected hemi-field can act as an effective CS in a Pavlovian conditioning task.
source: These results show that a visual cue presented in the V1 lesion-affected hemi-field can act as an effective CS in a Pavlovian conditioning task.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the behavioral data presented.

claim: The monkeys were able to discriminate successfully between the difference in the magnitude and timing of reward predicted by CSs according to where they were presented in the lesion-affected hemi-field.
source: Moreover, the monkeys were able to discriminate successfully between the difference in the magnitude and timing of reward predicted by CSs according to where they were presented in the lesion-affected hemi-field.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from the behavioral data showing differential responses to LR-CS and SR-CS.

claim: After the switching of CS positions, the high conditioned licking rate gradually changed to follow the new LR-CS, irrespective of whether the CSs were presented in both intact and lesion-affected visual fields.
source: After the switching, the high conditioned licking rate gradually changed to follow the new LR-CS, again irrespective of whether the CSs were presented in both intact and lesion-affected visual fields (Figure 1F).
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral results during reversal learning with reference to figure.

claim: Monkeys can flexibly associate the locations of the visual CSs and the reward predicted by them even without V1.
source: These results indicate that monkeys can flexibly associate the locations of the visual CSs and the reward predicted by them even without V1.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from reversal learning data.

claim: Muscimol (0.5 μL; 1 μg/μL concentration at a rate of 1 μL/15 s) was injected into the ipsi-lesional SC of monkeys K and T.
source: To investigate whether visual processing in the SC was responsible for the expression of visually-evoked conditioned responses when the CSs were presented to the V1 lesion affected side, the GABA agonist muscimol (0.5 μL; 1 μg/μL concentration at a rate of 1 μL/15 s) was injected into the ipsi-lesional SC of monkeys K and T.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure with specific parameters.

claim: The suppressive effect of the muscimol injection was confirmed by showing that the monkey failed to make saccades to the LR-CS location as previously shown for the blindsight monkeys by Kato et al. (2011).
source: The suppressive effect of the muscimol injection was confirmed by showing that the monkey failed to make saccades to the LR-CS location as previously shown for the blindsight monkeys by Kato et al. (2011) (Figure 2B; see disappearance of saccades to the left-upward target).
evidence: Direct statement of control experiment with citation and reference to figure.

claim: Before the SC inactivation, anticipatory licking evoked by the LR-CS presentation served as a baseline control in the Pavlovian conditioning task.
source: Also, before the muscimol injection, anticipatory licking evoked by the LR-CS presentation (0–0.7 or 1.3 ms) served as a baseline control in our Pavlovian conditioning task (Figure 2C left).
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design with reference to figure.

claim: Over 20–30 min following the muscimol injection, the normal conditioned response (anticipatory licking) gradually disappeared.
source: However, over the next 20–30 min the normal conditioned response (anticipatory licking) gradually disappeared (Figure 2C right).
evidence: Direct statement of temporal dynamics of muscimol effect with reference to figure.

claim: In monkey T, all anticipatory response was abolished after SC inactivation and licking appeared only after the juice reward was delivered.
source: At which point, two new patterns of behaviour were observed: (i) in the case of monkey T (Figure 2C right), all anticipatory response was abolished and licking appeared only after the juice reward was delivered
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral observation with reference to figure.

claim: For monkey K, anticipatory licking was evoked shortly after the onset of both the LR-CS and SR-CS after SC inactivation.
source: and (ii) for monkey K anticipatory licking was evoked shortly after the onset of both the LR-CS and SR-CS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1.
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral observation with reference to figure.

claim: The animal's ability to discriminate between the CSs on the basis of position within the visual field was lost after SC inactivation in monkey K.
source: In other words, the animal's ability to discriminate between the CSs on the basis of position within the visual field was lost.
evidence: Direct interpretation of the behavioral data from monkey K.

claim: Muscimol injections were administered in 13 experiments (monkey K: 9 experiments, monkey T: 4 experiments).
source: Muscimol injections were administered in 13 experiments (monkey K: 9 experiments, monkey T: 4 experiments).
evidence: Direct statement of sample size.

claim: Before the SC inactivation, monkeys licked a reward spout more frequently during CS period in LR trials than in SR trials in all sessions.
source: Before the SC inactivation (control), monkeys licked a reward spout more frequently during CS period in LR trials than in SR trials in all sessions.
evidence: Direct statement of behavioral results across all sessions.

claim: The difference of the licking rate between in LR trials and in SR trials was diminished after SC inactivation (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test; p<0.001).
source: The difference of the licking rate between in LR trials and in SR trials was diminished after SC inactivation (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test; p<0.001).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result with specific test and p-value.

claim: During the SC inactivation, the difference of licking rate was not significantly different from zero (one-sample t-test; p>0.005).
source: During the SC inactivation, the difference of licking rate was not significantly different from zero (one-sample t-test; p>0.005).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result with specific test and p-value.

claim: The visual processing signifying CS onset by the SC on the V1 lesion-affected side was essential for a previously established conditioned response to be expressed in the Pavlovian conditioning task.
source: These results indicate that the visual processing signifying CS onset by the SC on the V1 lesion-affected side was essential for a previously established conditioned response to be expressed in our Pavlovian conditioning task.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from SC inactivation experiments.

claim: Dopamine neurons are phasically activated by unpredicted conditioned stimuli in Pavlovian tasks.
source: It has been reported widely that dopamine neurons are phasically activated by unpredicted conditioned stimuli in Pavlovian tasks (Schultz, 1998).
evidence: Statement of established finding with citation.

claim: Neurons included in the sample had low baseline firing rates (<10 Hz).
source: The neurons included in our sample therefore had low baseline firing rates (<10 Hz), and broad spike-widths (>0.45 ms between the first negative peak and next positive peak) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Direct statement of electrophysiological criteria with reference to figures.

claim: Neurons included in the sample had broad spike-widths (>0.45 ms between the first negative peak and next positive peak).
source: The neurons included in our sample therefore had low baseline firing rates (<10 Hz), and broad spike-widths (>0.45 ms between the first negative peak and next positive peak) (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Direct statement of electrophysiological criteria with reference to figures.

claim: The location of recorded neurons was confirmed by identifying the site of small lesions made at some of the recording sites in tissue immunostained for tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: The location of recorded neurons was later confirmed by identifying the site of small lesions made at some of the recording sites in tissue immunostained for tyrosine hydroxylase (Figure 3D).
evidence: Direct statement of histological verification with reference to figure.

claim: Putative DA neurons were activated robustly by the onset of the fixation point.
source: First, because of its task-relevance and unpredictability, putative DA neurons were activated robustly by the onset of the fixation point.
evidence: Direct statement of electrophysiological observation.

claim: The DA response to fixation point was similar in LR trials and SR trials because at the time the fixation point was presented the magnitude and timing of reward predicted by the upcoming CS was unknown.
source: However, this response was similar in LR trials and SR trials (left-hand panels of Figure 3F and G) because at the time the fixation point was presented the magnitude and timing of reward predicted by the upcoming CS was unknown.
evidence: Direct statement of observation with mechanistic explanation.

claim: When the temporally uncertain CSs were presented, a clear difference in the putative dopamine response was evident between the LR and SR trials – a reliably larger response was evoked by the LR-CS.
source: Subsequently, when the temporally uncertain CSs were presented, a clear difference in the putative dopamine response was evident between the LR and SR trials – a reliably larger response was evoked by the LR-CS (central panels of Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Direct statement of electrophysiological observation with reference to figures.

claim: Responses to predicted presentations of the juice reward were unreliable and significantly weaker than responses evoked either by the FP or CSs.
source: In this case, responses to predicted presentations of the juice reward were unreliable and significantly weaker than responses evoked either by the FP or CSs (right-hand panels of Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Direct statement of electrophysiological observation with reference to figures.

claim: There was no reliable difference between the putative dopamine responses evoked by FP presentation in LR and SR trials (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test).
source: The left-hand panel shows that there was no reliable difference between the putative dopamine responses evoked by FP presentation in LR and SR trials (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical result with specific test.

claim: The LR-CS elicited a significantly larger responses compared with those evoked by the SR-CS.
source: However, the LR-CS elicited a significantly larger responses compared with those evoked by the SR-CS (central panel Figure 3H).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with reference to figure.

claim: DA responses to CSs were not strongly affected by the V1 lesion.
source: These responses were not strongly affected by the V1 lesion.
evidence: Direct statement of observation comparing responses in intact vs. lesion-affected fields.

claim: Firing rate of the responses to CSs presented into lesion affected and intact visual fields were not significantly different.
source: Firing rate of the responses to CSs presented into lesion affected and intact visual fields were not significantly different (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with reference to figure.

claim: There were no reliable differences in the responses evoked by the onset of the predicted LR or SR.
source: Finally, there were no reliable differences in the responses evoked by the onset of the predicted LR or SR (right-hand panel Figure 3H).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with reference to figure.

claim: The overall mean response latency was 107 ms.
source: The overall mean response latency was 107 ms while the latencies of the individual neurons were distributed between 60 to 160 ms after the LR-CS onset (latency = the time when the neural response rate exceeded 2SD of their baseline activity).
evidence: Direct statement of measured latency with definition.

claim: The latencies of the individual neurons were distributed between 60 to 160 ms after the LR-CS onset.
source: The overall mean response latency was 107 ms while the latencies of the individual neurons were distributed between 60 to 160 ms after the LR-CS onset (latency = the time when the neural response rate exceeded 2SD of their baseline activity).
evidence: Direct statement of measured latency range with definition.

claim: The earliest time points when response differentiation lasting more than 15 ms started was 122 ms from the CS onset in lesion-affected visual field.
source: The earliest time points when response differentiation lasting more than 15 ms started was 122 ms from the CS onset in lesion-affected visual field, and 112 ms in intact visual field (Figure 3I).
evidence: Direct statement of measured timing with reference to figure.

claim: The earliest time points when response differentiation lasting more than 15 ms started was 112 ms from the CS onset in intact visual field.
source: The earliest time points when response differentiation lasting more than 15 ms started was 122 ms from the CS onset in lesion-affected visual field, and 112 ms in intact visual field (Figure 3I).
evidence: Direct statement of measured timing with reference to figure.

claim: The latency of the reward discrimination by DA neurons was minimally affected by the absence of V1.
source: This result indicates that the latency of the reward discrimination by DA neurons was minimally affected by the absence of V1.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from comparison of latencies in intact vs. lesion-affected fields.

claim: In the absence of V1, temporally unpredicted visual CSs were able to elicit typical short latency and short duration phasic responses in ventral midbrain neurons, presumed to be dopaminergic.
source: These results showed in the absence of V1, that temporally unpredicted visual CSs were able to elicit typical short latency and short duration phasic responses in ventral midbrain neurons, presumed to be dopaminergic.
evidence: Direct conclusion summarizing the electrophysiological findings.

claim: DA neurons could discriminate the LR-CS and SR-CS, based on the location of their presentation within the lesion-affected visual field.
source: These neurons could discriminate the LR-CS and SR-CS, based on the location of their presentation within the lesion-affected visual field.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from differential DA responses to LR-CS vs. SR-CS.

claim: The residual early visual structures (most likely the midbrain SC) retained the capacity to evoke differential phasic DA responses informed by the reward expected from CS.
source: These results indicate that the residual early visual structures (most likely the midbrain SC) retained the capacity to evoke differential phasic DA responses informed by the reward expected from CS.
evidence: Direct conclusion with inference about the likely neural substrate.

claim: After the collection of control data, baseline records of the responses of the DA neurons to the presentation of the fixation point, CS and reward were recorded before muscimol injection.
source: Thus, after the collection of control data on visually guided saccadic task and on Pavlovian conditioning task, baseline records of the responses of the DA neurons to the presentation of the fixation point, CS and reward were recorded.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental procedure.

claim: The activity of a single DA neuron was recorded both before and after the muscimol injection.
source: Thus, the activity of a single DA neuron was recorded both before and after the muscimol injection.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental design.

claim: Only when the DA waveforms remained constant before and after muscimol injection were the data included in the sample.
source: To ensure that the same recorded neuron was maintained throughout the session (that is, for approximately 1.5 hr), its waveform was carefully monitored. Only when the DA waveforms remained constant before, after muscimol injection were the data included in our sample (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Direct statement of inclusion criteria with reference to figure.

claim: Before collicular inactivation, the DA responses to the task-related stimuli were similar to those observed in previous experiments.
source: Before collicular inactivation (Figure 4A) the DA responses to the task-related stimuli were similar to those observed in previous experiments (see above – Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Direct statement comparing current results to earlier findings with reference to figures.

claim: After the injection of muscimol, when the relevant SC was inactivated, the robust response evoked by the FP was largely unaffected.
source: After the injection of muscimol, when the relevant SC was inactivated, the robust response evoked by the FP was largely unaffected (compare Figure 4A and B (left-hand panels), Figure 4C left and 4D left, Wilcoxon test, not significantly different).
evidence: Direct statement of observation with statistical test and reference to figures.

claim: After the muscimol injection the response of the recorded neuron to presentation of the LR-CS was retained for a short while.
source: After the muscimol injection the response of the recorded neuron to presentation of the LR-CS was retained for a short while (central panels Figure 4B).
evidence: Direct statement of temporal dynamics with reference to figure.

claim: After a few trials following muscimol injection, the drug action became apparent, and the CS-evoked response was almost completely abolished.
source: However, after a few trials the drug action became apparent, and the CS-evoked response was almost completely abolished (central panel Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Direct statement of observation with reference to figures.

claim: In early trials after muscimol injection, when the reward delivery was still predicted by visual input from the SC, reward presentation failed to evoke a phasic DA response.
source: It is also significant that in these early trials, when the reward delivery was still predicted by visual input from the SC, reward presentation failed to evoke a phasic DA response.
evidence: Direct statement of observation with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: As the colliculus became fully inhibited, the now unpredicted presentation of the reward evoked a robust phasic response.
source: However, as the colliculus became fully inhibited, the now unpredicted presentation of the reward evoked a robust phasic response, which in this case was clearly dependent on the magnitude and timing of reward predicted by the CS.
evidence: Direct statement of observation with mechanistic interpretation.

claim: The pattern of DA response during SC inactivation was consistent in all recorded neurons.
source: This pattern of response was consistent in all recorded neurons (Figure 4D).
evidence: Direct statement of consistency across sample with reference to figure.

claim: For most of the recorded neurons, reward responses emerged as the inactivation progressed.
source: Also, for most of the recorded neurons, reward responses emerged as the inactivation progressed (right panels of Figure 4B, C and D).
evidence: Direct statement of observation with reference to figures.

claim: In SR trials, firing rate to CS was unaltered by the muscimol injection.
source: In SR trials, firing rate to CS was unaltered by the injection.
evidence: Direct statement of observation.

claim: During the SC inactivation, DA responses evoked by the CS were not significantly different between LR and SR trials.
source: During the SC inactivation, DA responses evoked by the CS were not significantly different between LR and SR trials (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of statistical comparison with reference to figure.

claim: In the absence of V1, visual signals signifying CS onset, with the capacity to elicit a short latency phasic response in presumed DA neurons, are most likely to be relayed via the direct retino-tecto-nigral projection.
source: Together, these results confirm that, in the absence of V1, visual signals signifying CS onset, with the capacity to elicit a short latency phasic response in presumed DA neurons, are most likely to be relayed via the direct retino-tecto-nigral projection (Comoli et al., 2003; Dommett et al., 2005), although an indirect contribution, possibly involving the pedunculopontine nucleus cannot be ruled out at present (Harting, 1977; Redgrave et al., 1987); Kobayashi and Okada, 2007).
evidence: Direct conclusion with supporting citations and acknowledgment of alternative possibilities.

claim: An indirect contribution, possibly involving the pedunculopontine nucleus cannot be ruled out at present.
source: Together, these results confirm that, in the absence of V1, visual signals signifying CS onset, with the capacity to elicit a short latency phasic response in presumed DA neurons, are most likely to be relayed via the direct retino-tecto-nigral projection (Comoli et al., 2003; Dommett et al., 2005), although an indirect contribution, possibly involving the pedunculopontine nucleus cannot be ruled out at present (Harting, 1977; Redgrave et al., 1987); Kobayashi and Okada, 2007).
evidence: Direct acknowledgment of alternative explanation with citations.

claim: Presentation of a CS was equally capable of eliciting a robust conditioned response when it was presented either to the V1 lesion-affected visual field, or to the field served both by an intact visual cortex and the SC.
source: The main findings of the present study were, first, that after several days of training, presentation of a CS was equally capable of eliciting a robust conditioned response when it was presented either to the V1 lesion-affected visual field, or to the field served both by an intact visual cortex and the SC.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding.

claim: The capacity of residual subcortical visual pathways to elicit Pavlovian conditioned responses was demonstrated.
source: This result demonstrated the capacity of residual subcortical visual pathways to elicit Pavlovian conditioned responses.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from behavioral data.

claim: When identical CSs that predicted different amounts of primary reward were presented at different locations, either within the intact or lesion-affected visual fields, differential conditioned responses were elicited.
source: Secondly, when identical CSs that predicted different amounts of primary reward (juice) were presented at different locations, either within the intact or lesion-affected visual fields, differential conditioned responses were elicited.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding.

claim: The subcortical neural mechanisms responsible for mediating the conditioned responses can discriminate CSs on the basis of spatial location.
source: This suggests that the subcortical neural mechanisms responsible for mediating the conditioned responses can discriminate CSs on the basis of spatial location.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from behavioral data showing differential responses.

claim: A critical involvement of the SC was established by showing that anticipatory conditioned responding reflecting reward expectation was disrupted when the critical locus representing the LR-CS within the spatial retinotopic map in the SC was locally inactivated with muscimol.
source: Thirdly, a critical involvement of the SC was established by showing that anticipatory conditioned responding reflecting reward expectation was disrupted when the critical locus representing the LR-CS within the spatial retinotopic map in the SC was locally inactivated with muscimol.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding from inactivation experiments.

claim: Visual CSs presented to the lesion-affected visual field elicited patterns of phasic responses in putative DA neurons that have been widely reported by others.
source: Fourthly, parallel electrophysiological recording from putative DA neurons revealed that visual CSs presented to the lesion-affected visual field elicited patterns of phasic responses that have been widely reported by others.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding with reference to literature.

claim: The initial task-relevant fixation point evoked robust DA responses that were independent of subsequent CS value.
source: Specifically, the initial task-relevant fixation point evoked robust DA responses that were independent of subsequent CS value (Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Matsumoto and Takada, 2013)
evidence: Direct statement of observation with supporting citations.

claim: The temporally unpredicted CSs evoked phasic DA responses that were dependent on the predictive value of the CS.
source: the temporally unpredicted CSs evoked phasic DA responses that were dependent on the predictive value of the CS (Tobler et al., 2005; Fiorillo, 2013)
evidence: Direct statement of observation with supporting citations.

claim: The predicted reward deliveries evoked only muted responses.
source: while the predicted reward deliveries evoked only muted responses (Schultz, 1998).
evidence: Direct statement of observation with supporting citation.

claim: Phasic DA responses evoked by CS were almost completely abolished when the CS representation in the colliculus was pharmacologically blocked.
source: Finally, phasic DA responses evoked by CS were almost completely abolished when the CS representation in the colliculus was pharmacologically blocked.
evidence: Direct statement of main finding from inactivation experiments.

claim: The SC was critically involved in the short-latency activation of DA neurons by visual CSs presented to the V1 lesion-affected visual field.
source: Thus, the SC was critically involved in the short-latency activation of DA neurons by visual CSs presented to the V1 lesion-affected visual field.
evidence: Direct conclusion drawn from inactivation experiments.

claim: Visual cues presented to the lesion-affected field in monkeys with a unilateral V1 lesion can support behavioral Pavlovian conditioning, and elicit DA responses that reflect the reward predicted by the CS via an afferent projection route involving the midbrain SC.
source: Together these results show that visual cues presented to the lesion-affected field in monkeys with a unilateral V1 lesion can support behavioral Pavlovian conditioning, and elicit DA responses that reflect the reward predicted by the CS via an afferent projection route involving the midbrain SC.
evidence: Direct summary of main conclusions.

claim: Midbrain DA neurons causally contribute to reinforcement learning.
source: Many studies have indicated that midbrain DA neurons causally contribute to reinforcement learning.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge from literature.

claim: When reward expectation signals from DA neurons were impaired by D1 receptor blocker or when NMDA receptors were knocked out in DA receptor expressing neurons in various brain areas, conditioned response was impaired in many kinds of behavioral learning tasks.
source: For example, when reward expectation signals from DA neurons were impaired by D1 receptor blocker or when NMDA receptors were knocked out in DA receptor expressing neurons in various brain areas, conditioned response was impaired in many kinds of behavioral learning tasks (Di Ciano et al., 2001; Flagel et al., 2011; Parker et al., 2010, 2011; Puig and Miller, 2012; Berridge and Robinson, 1998).
evidence: Statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: When DA neurons or neurons expressing D1 receptors were activated by electrical or optogenetical stimulation, various forms of conditioned behaviour were induced.
source: Alternatively, when DA neurons or neurons expressing D1 receptors were activated by electrical or optogenetical stimulation, various forms of conditioned behaviour were induced (Olds and Milner, 1954; Adamantidis et al., 2011; Ilango et al., 2014; Steinberg et al., 2013; Kravitz et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of findings from cited literature.

claim: It remains unclear how DA neurons are able to signal the value or salience of unpredicted objects or events at short-latency.
source: Thus, such involvement of dopaminergic transmission or DA neuron activity in learning has been well studied, however, it remains unclear how DA neurons are able to signal the value or salience of unpredicted objects or events at short-latency.
evidence: Statement of knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The early phasic responses of DA neurons have two separable components; an early non-selective sensory response that represents temporal salient-event prediction errors, and a second component that codes the object/event's reward value.
source: It has been proposed that the early phasic responses of DA neurons have two separable components; an early non-selective sensory response that represents temporal salient-event prediction errors, and a second component that codes the object/event's reward value (Joshua et al., 2009; Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Schultz, 2016).
evidence: Statement of hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: Response latencies in V1 following the onset of a visual CS are typically in the range 40–60 ms.
source: Following the onset of a visual CS response latencies in V1 are typically in the range 40–60 ms, while in the inferotemporal cortex where objects/events are identified they are slower in the range 80–100 ms (Thorpe and Fabre-Thorpe, 2001).
evidence: Statement of established timing from cited literature.

claim: In the inferotemporal cortex where objects/events are identified, response latencies are slower in the range 80–100 ms.
source: Following the onset of a visual CS response latencies in V1 are typically in the range 40–60 ms, while in the inferotemporal cortex where objects/events are identified they are slower in the range 80–100 ms (Thorpe and Fabre-Thorpe, 2001).
evidence: Statement of established timing from cited literature.

claim: There are no obvious direct connections from inferotemporal cortex to the ventral midbrain.
source: Moreover, since there are no obvious direct connections to the ventral midbrain, the results of cortical visual processing are likely to be relayed via additional time consuming indirect routes.
evidence: Statement of anatomical knowledge with inference about timing implications.

claim: Response latencies in the retino-recipient midbrain SC are significantly less (40–50 ms).
source: On the other hand, response latencies in the retino-recipient midbrain SC are significantly less (40–50 ms) and there is a direct tectonigral projection to substantia nigra pars compacta (Comoli et al., 2003; McHaffie et al., 2006; May et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement of established timing and anatomy from cited literature.

claim: There is a direct tectonigral projection to substantia nigra pars compacta.
source: On the other hand, response latencies in the retino-recipient midbrain SC are significantly less (40–50 ms) and there is a direct tectonigral projection to substantia nigra pars compacta (Comoli et al., 2003; McHaffie et al., 2006; May et al., 2009).
evidence: Statement of established anatomy from cited literature.

claim: The earliest sensory component of the phasic DA response (70–150 ms) is probably mediated via subcortical visual processing involving the SC.

claim: The initial component of the phasic DA response is a non-selective salience signal that represents a temporal salient-event prediction error.
source: The first is that the initial component of the phasic DA response is a non-selective salience signal that represents a temporal salient-event prediction error (Joshua et al 2009, Bromberg-Martin et al., 2010; Schultz, 2016).
evidence: Statement of hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: The second phasic component is value-coded and takes longer to compute because the unexpected event needs to be identified before its value is known.
source: The second phasic component is value-coded and takes longer to compute because the unexpected event needs to be identified before its value is known.

claim: Stimulus identification frequently requires stimulus detection, foveation and cortical analysis of geometric form, colour, texture, and apparent motion, in various permutations and combinations.
source: Stimulus identification frequently requires stimulus detection, foveation and cortical analysis of geometric form, colour, texture, and apparent motion, in various permutations and combinations (Nomoto et al., 2010).

claim: In the case of simple stimuli (for example, luminance change at different spatial locations) the non-selective salience and value components can merge to a near unimodal response that, in some cases, can be separated by sophisticated mathematical analysis.
source: However, in the case of simple stimuli (for example, luminance change at different spatial locations) it is suggested that the non-selective salience and value components can merge to a near unimodal response that, in some cases, can be separated by sophisticated mathematical analysis (Fiorillo et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement of hypothesis from cited literature.

claim: For both subcortical salience and cortical stimulus identification the early sensory responses have to be relayed through an unspecified 'value-decoder' that communicates with DA neurons, thereby enabling them to report reward prediction errors.
source: This version suggests that for both subcortical salience and cortical stimulus identification the early sensory responses have to be relayed through an unspecified 'value-decoder' that communicates with DA neurons, thereby enabling them to report reward prediction errors (Schultz, 2016).

source: Uchida and colleagues recently identified all the brain regions which project to DA neurons in rodents.

claim: Brain regions that project to DA neurons include the striatum, amygdala, subthalamic nucleus, pedunculopontine nucleus, rostromedial reticular nucleus, and GABAergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars reticulata.
source: They report afferent connections from the striatum, amygdala, subthalamic nucleus, pedunculopontine nucleus, rostromedial reticular nucleus, and GABAergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars reticulata (Watabe-Uchida et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement of anatomical findings from cited literature.

claim: There are many possible locations that receive input from primary visual structures, compute stimulus value and communicate this to DA neurons in the ventral midbrain.
source: Consequently, there are many possible locations that receive input from primary visual structures, compute stimulus value and communicate this to DA neurons in the ventral midbrain.

claim: Indirect routes of communication can offer a perfectly reasonable explanation for the value coding of the second delayed component of the early phasic DA response.
source: These indirect routes of communication can offer a perfectly reasonable explanation for the value coding of the second delayed component of the early phasic DA response.

claim: The earliest component (70–150 ms) of phasic DA response is not always best described as a value insensitive salience signal.
source: However, it is important to note that the earliest component (70–150 ms) of phasic DA response is not always best described as a value insensitive salience signal.
evidence: Statement challenging a hypothesis based on current and cited data.

claim: When CSs can be discriminated on the basis of luminance change at different locations (a subcortical collicular visual competence), the phasic DA response latencies are frequently around 100 ms (pre-gaze shift), unimodal and clearly code the predictive value of the CS.
source: Both the present results (where cortical visual processing is impaired), and earlier studies of Schultz and his colleagues involving intact monkeys (Tobler et al., 2005; Fiorillo, 2013) report that when CSs can be discriminated on the basis of luminance change at different locations (a subcortical collicular visual competence – Boehnke and Munoz, 2008), the phasic DA response latencies are frequently around 100 ms (pre-gaze shift), unimodal and clearly code the predictive value of the CS.
evidence: Statement integrating current results with cited literature.

claim: Visual response latencies in intermediary structures are too long (typically >100 ms) to account for value coding of a unimodal phasic DA response that peaks at about 100 ms.
source: Visual response latencies in intermediary structures identified above are too long (typically >100 ms) to account for value coding of a unimodal phasic DA response that peaks at about 100 ms.
evidence: Inference based on timing considerations.

claim: The predictive value of a visual CS may already be encoded in the early sensory response of both the cortical and subcortical early visual systems.
source: The proposal is that the predictive value of a visual CS may already be encoded in the early sensory response of both the cortical and subcortical early visual systems.
evidence: Statement of alternative hypothesis.

claim: An association with, or an expectation of reward can dramatically influence the magnitude of the initial sensory response in early sensory areas throughout the brain.
source: For example, there are many papers that demonstrate that an association with, or an expectation of reward can dramatically influence the magnitude of the initial sensory response in early sensory areas throughout the brain (Mogami and Tanaka, 2006; Serences and Saproo, 2010; Metzger et al., 2006; Leathers and Olson, 2012), including the SC (Ikeda and Hikosaka, 2003).

claim: An association with, or an expectation of reward can dramatically influence the magnitude of the initial sensory response in the SC.
source: For example, there are many papers that demonstrate that an association with, or an expectation of reward can dramatically influence the magnitude of the initial sensory response in early sensory areas throughout the brain (Mogami and Tanaka, 2006; Serences and Saproo, 2010; Metzger et al., 2006; Leathers and Olson, 2012), including the SC (Ikeda and Hikosaka, 2003).
evidence: Statement of established findings from cited literature.

claim: The most parsimonious explanation of how the earliest responses of DA neurons can be value-coded is that they receive input from the SC that has been already value-coded through a classically conditioned process of sensory pre-tuning of the CS value in early sensory structures.
source: The most parsimonious explanation of how the earliest responses of DA neurons can be value-coded is, therefore, that they receive input from the SC that has been already value-coded through a classically conditioned process of sensory pre-tuning of the CS value in early sensory structures (Ikeda and Hikosaka, 2003).
evidence: Statement of proposed mechanism with supporting citation.

claim: In the present study and those of others, stimuli are conditioned by Pavlovian association with different levels/probabilities of reward, prior to the recording of DA neurons.
source: Thus, in our study and those of others, stimuli are conditioned by Pavlovian association with different levels/probabilities of reward, prior to the recording of DA neurons (Fiorillo et al., 2003; Tobler et al., 2005; Matsumoto and Hikosaka, 2009).

source: The likely effect of this process would be to tune the initial sensory responses in early visual structures to reflect the reward predicted by the CS.

source: According to this suggestion, if the object/event prediction error detected in early visual structures has been value-coded by prior Pavlovian association, the event prediction error would also be a reward prediction error.

source: In the case of the SC, if a value-coded signal evoked by a CS was relayed to the DA neurons via the tectonigral projection (Comoli et al., 2003; Dommett et al., 2005; McHaffie et al., 2006; May et al., 2009), it would explain how DA neurons can signal reward prediction errors with latencies in the range 70–150 ms (present study and Fiorillo et al., 2003; Tobler et al., 2005).

evidence: Inference about mechanism with supporting citation.
